title: Chapter 8 Drill: Demyelinating, Autoimmune, Paraneoplastic, and Infectious Disorders

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis notes that her leg weakness and blurred vision return each time she takes a hot bath, and resolve within an hour. What is the best interpretation?
options: Transient conduction block in demyelinated axons from raised temperature, not a new relapse
A new inflammatory relapse that requires intravenous corticosteroids
Conversion to a progressive phenotype
A medication adverse effect requiring drug withdrawal
items.explanation: Uhthoff phenomenon is a reversible worsening of existing deficits when core temperature rises, because heat worsens conduction in demyelinated fibers. It is a pseudorelapse that resolves with cooling, so steroids are unnecessary. It carries no implication for progression, and no drug is implicated, so the best step is reassurance and cooling strategies. Reassurance, cooling vests, and avoiding hot environments are appropriate, and a true relapse requires new or worsening deficits lasting more than 24 hours without fever.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis for 12 years has had three years of gradual gait decline. He has had no relapses and MRI shows no new lesions. What is the best classification?
options: Primary progressive multiple sclerosis
Relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis in remission
Secondary progressive multiple sclerosis
Radiologically isolated syndrome
items.explanation: A relapsing course followed by gradual accumulation of disability independent of attacks defines secondary progressive disease. Primary progressive disease requires progression from onset. Remission would mean stability, not worsening, and radiologically isolated syndrome applies only to asymptomatic imaging findings. The distinction matters because progressive disease responds to different treatments. Progression independent of relapse activity is now recognized across phenotypes, and secondary progression is usually diagnosed retrospectively after a period of confirmed worsening.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis has had no improvement after high-dose steroids and immunoglobulin for two weeks, and no tumor was found. What is the next step?
options: Repeat the same first-line therapy for another six months
Second-line immunotherapy such as rituximab or cyclophosphamide
Withdraw all immunotherapy and observe the patient clinically for relapse
Start long-term benzodiazepines alone for symptom control
items.explanation: Autoimmune encephalitis is treated with steroids, immunoglobulin, or plasma exchange first, and patients without clear improvement after about two weeks move to rituximab or cyclophosphamide, which improves outcomes. Repeating the same therapy delays recovery, and withdrawal or symptomatic therapy alone leaves the disease untreated. Early escalation is linked to better outcomes, and long-term maintenance and relapse monitoring are then planned according to the antibody and tumor findings.

items.stem: A 40-year-old Black woman has bilateral facial palsy, hilar lymphadenopathy, and leptomeningeal enhancement. CSF shows low glucose and lymphocytes. What is the best initial treatment once infection is excluded?
options: High-dose corticosteroids
Intravenous acyclovir
Rituximab as the first agent
Anticoagulation with warfarin
items.explanation: The picture suggests neurosarcoidosis, which is treated first with high-dose corticosteroids, with steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate or infliximab for refractory disease. Acyclovir targets herpes viruses, rituximab is not first-line, and anticoagulation addresses thrombosis, which is not the problem. Gadolinium enhancement of the leptomeninges and cranial nerves, and a high CSF angiotensin converting enzyme or hilar adenopathy, support the diagnosis, and tissue confirmation is sought.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis develops right leg weakness that limits walking over four days. She has no infection. What is the best treatment?
options: Oral prednisone at a low dose tapered gradually over six weeks
Intravenous immunoglobulin daily for five consecutive days total
High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone for three to five days
Start intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses immediately today
items.explanation: A disabling relapse is treated with high-dose corticosteroids, typically 1 gram of methylprednisolone daily for three to five days, which hastens recovery. A low-dose oral taper is less effective. Intravenous immunoglobulin lacks reliable benefit for relapses, and cyclophosphamide is not a standard relapse or disease therapy for this patient. Oral high-dose steroids have shown similar efficacy in studies, but intravenous dosing remains the usual teaching standard for severe attacks when infection has been excluded.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with AIDS has a CD4 count of 50 and subacute headache. Opening pressure is 38 cm of water, and CSF cryptococcal antigen is positive. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Fluconazole alone with no spinal fluid drainage, since it penetrates the brain well
Dexamethasone only to reduce the inflammatory response
Acetazolamide with no antifungal therapy for raised pressure
Amphotericin B with flucytosine, and serial lumbar punctures for raised pressure
items.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis is treated with induction amphotericin B plus flucytosine, and therapeutic lumbar punctures lower raised pressure, which is a major cause of morbidity. Fluconazole alone is inadequate for induction, steroids worsen outcomes, and acetazolamide does not treat the infection. Pressure is controlled with repeated lumbar punctures because persistent elevation causes vision loss and death, and fluconazole consolidation follows after the induction course is complete.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman received alemtuzumab for aggressive multiple sclerosis. Which monitoring plan is appropriate?
options: Annual brain MRI scans only, with no scheduled laboratory testing after the last infusion is given
Monthly blood counts, creatinine, and urinalysis for four years after the last dose
Quarterly lipid profile and cardiac echocardiography for five years total
Hepatitis C viral load every month for the first year after treatment
items.explanation: Alemtuzumab causes secondary autoimmunity in a large share of patients, including thyroid disease, immune thrombocytopenia, and anti-glomerular basement membrane disease. Monthly counts, creatinine, and urinalysis continue for 48 months after the last course, with periodic thyroid testing. Imaging alone misses these complications, and lipid or hepatitis C testing does not target them. Patients must be counseled that autoimmune complications can appear years after treatment, so monitoring is a commitment that continues well beyond the last infusion.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has persistent fatigue, poor concentration, and orthostatic tachycardia months after COVID-19. Examination and MRI are normal. What is the best approach?
options: Supportive and rehabilitative care with symptom-directed treatment
Long-term high-dose corticosteroids
Lumbar puncture followed by antiviral therapy
Immunoglobulin infusions as standard care
items.explanation: Neurologic symptoms after COVID-19 often include cognitive complaints, fatigue, and autonomic dysfunction with normal studies, and management is supportive with graded rehabilitation and treatment of dysautonomia and sleep problems. Steroids, empiric antivirals, and immunoglobulin lack proven benefit. Reassurance with a validated plan, treatment of sleep, mood, and orthostatic symptoms, and gradual return to activity form the evidence-supported approach for this condition.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 80 has a year of slowing, forgetfulness, and gait unsteadiness. MRI shows diffuse atrophy and no mass. What is the main treatment?
options: Corticosteroids alone given for several weeks
Intrathecal amphotericin with repeated punctures
Lifelong pyrimethamine prophylaxis
Optimized combination antiretroviral therapy
items.explanation: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder reflects CNS infection and inflammation, and treatment is effective combination antiretroviral therapy, often considering CNS penetration. Steroids do not control the virus, amphotericin treats cryptococcus, and pyrimethamine is used for toxoplasmosis, which would show enhancing lesions. Regimens are chosen to be effective in the central nervous system, and viral suppression often improves cognition, so adherence and drug interaction review are part of management.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman receiving natalizumab develops progressive aphasia and right hemiparesis over three weeks. MRI shows nonenhancing subcortical white matter lesions involving U fibers. What is the next step?
options: Increase the dose of natalizumab
Hold natalizumab and send CSF for JC virus PCR
Start high-dose methylprednisolone and continue treatment
Perform an urgent muscle biopsy
items.explanation: New cognitive or focal deficits on natalizumab with subcortical U fiber lesions suggest progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, and the drug is suspended while CSF JC virus PCR is obtained. Continuing therapy or giving steroids risks worsening infection. Muscle biopsy has no role. Prompt recognition is essential because early withdrawal and treatment of the infection improves survival, and delay while awaiting confirmation allows irreversible neurologic injury to accumulate.

items.stem: A 53-year-old man has recurrent headaches, multiple small infarcts in different territories, and beading of cerebral arteries on angiography. CSF is mildly inflammatory. What is the most definitive test?
options: Repeat catheter angiography
Serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy
Transthoracic echocardiography
items.explanation: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system is diagnosed definitively by biopsy showing vessel wall inflammation, because angiographic beading is nonspecific and overlaps with vasospasm and atherosclerosis. Sedimentation rate is typically normal and echocardiography only screens for emboli. Cerebral angiography and MRI have limited specificity, and biopsy also excludes infection, lymphoma, and amyloid angiopathy that mimic this presentation closely.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with aquaporin-4 positive NMOSD has severe vision loss after five days of high-dose methylprednisolone with no improvement. What is the best next step?
options: Switch to oral prednisone alone
Plasma exchange
Add interferon beta
Start natalizumab
items.explanation: Early plasma exchange after steroid failure improves outcomes in NMOSD attacks, and starting it promptly matters for visual and spinal recovery. Oral prednisone is weaker than the intravenous dose already tried. Interferon beta and natalizumab can worsen NMOSD and are not relapse treatments. Early treatment matters because recovery after an NMOSD attack is often incomplete, and delay in plasma exchange has been linked to worse visual and motor outcomes.

items.stem: A neuroradiologist reviews a brain MRI for suspected multiple sclerosis. Which lesion morphology is most characteristic and best supports the diagnosis?
options: Symmetric confluent white matter change sparing the subcortical U fibers
Cortical laminar necrosis with gyral enhancement
Multiple punctate lesions limited to the basal ganglia
Ovoid periventricular lesions oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles
items.explanation: Ovoid lesions radiating perpendicular to the ventricular surface (Dawson fingers) follow perivenular inflammation and are typical of multiple sclerosis. Symmetric confluent change suggests leukodystrophy or small vessel disease, cortical laminar necrosis suggests hypoxic or ischemic injury, and isolated basal ganglia punctate lesions point toward vascular or metabolic causes. Perivenular orientation reflects inflammation around small veins, which is why the finding is considered more specific than nonspecific white matter spots.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman has progressive axial stiffness and painful spasms triggered by sudden noise, with a high serum GAD65 antibody titer and type 1 diabetes. Which is the best initial symptomatic treatment?
options: Diazepam
Carbamazepine
Methotrexate alone
Levodopa
items.explanation: Stiff-person syndrome with high titer GAD65 antibodies responds to GABAergic drugs, and benzodiazepines such as diazepam and baclofen are first-line, with immunotherapy added for refractory cases. Carbamazepine is not effective, levodopa treats parkinsonism, and methotrexate alone does not relieve spasms. Immunotherapy may be added when symptoms persist, and patients should also be screened for associated autoimmune disease such as thyroid disorders and pernicious anemia.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman feels brief electric shocks down her spine and into her legs when she flexes her neck. Where is the responsible lesion most likely located?
options: Lateral corticospinal tract of the thoracic cord
Conus medullaris
Dorsal columns of the cervical spinal cord
Posterior roots of the cauda equina
items.explanation: Lhermitte sign reflects demyelination of the cervical dorsal columns, where neck flexion stretches hyperexcitable axons and triggers ectopic discharges. It is common in multiple sclerosis. A lateral corticospinal lesion causes weakness and spasticity, conus lesions cause sphincter and saddle findings, and cauda equina root disease produces radicular pain and areflexia. Other sensory phenomena such as the MS hug and trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult carry similar localizing and diagnostic weight in clinic.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with untreated AIDS has progressive right hemiparesis, and MRI shows nonenhancing asymmetric subcortical white matter lesions. CSF JC virus PCR is positive. What is the best treatment?
options: Intravenous cidofovir alone given for several weeks of therapy
High-dose methylprednisolone for a month to reduce all brain inflammation
Intravenous ganciclovir for suspected cytomegalovirus infection
Start combination antiretroviral therapy to restore immune function
items.explanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy has no proven antiviral therapy, and survival depends on immune reconstitution with antiretroviral therapy. Cidofovir has not shown benefit, and steroids are used only for immune reconstitution inflammation, not to treat the infection. Ganciclovir treats cytomegalovirus. Within weeks of therapy some patients develop immune reconstitution syndrome, but survival is best when immune function recovers, so therapy should not be delayed or withdrawn.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man has fever, aphasia, and a focal seizure. MRI shows left temporal T2 hyperintensity, and CSF shows lymphocytes and red cells. What is the correct management?
options: Wait for the CSF PCR confirmation of virus before starting any treatment
Start intravenous acyclovir immediately while awaiting CSF HSV PCR
Begin high-dose corticosteroids alone and reassess in two days
Give oral valacyclovir as an outpatient with close follow-up
items.explanation: Herpes simplex encephalitis has a high mortality without treatment, so empiric intravenous acyclovir begins before confirmation and continues until PCR is negative. Delay worsens outcomes, steroids alone do not treat the virus, and oral therapy is inadequate for CNS infection. Delay in therapy is the strongest predictor of poor outcome, and the diagnosis is later supported by temporal lobe changes on MRI and a positive PCR in cerebrospinal fluid.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has two weeks of fever, headache, and cranial neuropathy. MRI shows basal meningeal enhancement and hydrocephalus, and CSF shows lymphocytes with low glucose. What therapy is appropriate?
options: Ceftriaxone and vancomycin only
Amphotericin B alone
Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, with adjunctive dexamethasone
Albendazole with praziquantel
items.explanation: Tuberculous meningitis causes basal enhancement, hydrocephalus, and low CSF glucose, and the regimen is four antituberculous drugs with dexamethasone, which reduces mortality. Standard bacterial coverage, amphotericin B, and antiparasitic therapy do not address Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Treatment lasts many months, drug-induced liver injury must be monitored, and hydrocephalus may need shunting, while steroids reduce inflammatory complications such as infarcts and arachnoiditis.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with mild active relapsing multiple sclerosis plans to conceive within a year. Which therapy is the most appropriate choice?
options: Glatiramer acetate
Teriflunomide tablets
Fingolimod capsules
Cladribine tablets
items.explanation: Glatiramer acetate has extensive pregnancy exposure data without evidence of harm and is considered a reasonable option when conception is planned. Teriflunomide is teratogenic and needs elimination, fingolimod is discontinued before conception, and cladribine is contraindicated in pregnancy and requires contraception for months after treatment. Planning matters because reliable contraception, timing of conception, and drug washout differ widely among disease therapies, so choice should be made before pregnancy, not after.

items.stem: A college student develops meningococcal meningitis. Which step applies to her roommate?
options: No intervention is necessary because the disease is not contagious
Chemoprophylaxis with rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone
Supportive care alone for fourteen days of observation
Prophylactic acyclovir given for several days
items.explanation: Close contacts of meningococcal disease, including household and dormitory contacts, should receive chemoprophylaxis promptly, using rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone. Doing nothing leaves risk, supportive care alone does not prevent infection, and acyclovir has no activity against bacteria. Contacts include household members and anyone with direct exposure to oral secretions, and vaccination of close contacts is also considered, depending on the serogroup identified.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman taking natalizumab for three years tests positive for JC virus antibodies and previously received mitoxantrone. Which statement best describes her risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy?
options: Low, because natalizumab has no effect on viral surveillance
Eliminated by monthly MRI alone
High, because she has all three major risk factors
Unchanged by prior immunosuppressant exposure
items.explanation: The three established risk factors are anti-JC virus antibody positivity, treatment longer than about two years, and prior immunosuppressant use, and risk rises sharply when all are present. The antibody index adds stratification. MRI surveillance can detect early lesions but does not eliminate risk. Prior immunosuppression clearly adds to risk, so her risk is not low or unchanged.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has a first episode of unilateral painful optic neuritis. Which baseline finding best predicts her later risk of multiple sclerosis?
options: Severity of the initial visual loss at onset
Presence of optic disc swelling at presentation
Age of the patient at the first episode
T2 white matter lesions on brain MRI
items.explanation: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial showed that brain MRI lesions at presentation are the strongest predictor of later multiple sclerosis, with risk rising with lesion number. Severity of visual loss and disc swelling do not predict conversion, and absence of disc swelling, with pain on eye movement, is more typical of multiple sclerosis than of other causes.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has urinary urgency, and bladder ultrasound shows a post-void residual of 250 mL. Which management is best?
options: Intermittent self-catheterization, with or without an anticholinergic
Anticholinergic therapy alone to reduce urgency
Indwelling catheter for life
Fluid restriction to under one liter a day
items.explanation: A large residual in multiple sclerosis suggests detrusor sphincter dyssynergia with incomplete emptying, and intermittent catheterization reduces infection and renal risk. An anticholinergic alone could worsen retention. A permanent indwelling catheter carries a higher infection risk, and fluid restriction concentrates urine without treating the cause. Renal ultrasound and periodic urinary tract infection surveillance protect the upper tracts, and urology referral is appropriate when residual volumes remain high despite treatment.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man had one episode of brainstem demyelination. MRI shows lesions in two typical regions but none enhancing, and no earlier clinical event. Which result would allow the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis at this visit?
options: Elevated serum neurofilament light chain showing ongoing axonal injury in the disease
A normal CSF IgG index with a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis of under 10 cells
CSF specific oligoclonal bands, which can substitute for dissemination in time
Positive visual evoked potentials with delayed P100 latency in the affected eye
items.explanation: In the 2017 McDonald criteria, CSF oligoclonal bands unique to the spinal fluid can stand in for dissemination in time in a patient with a typical clinically isolated syndrome and dissemination in space. Evoked potentials and serum neurofilament are not part of the criteria, and a normal IgG index with mild pleocytosis does not show intrathecal synthesis.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has a 3 cm brain lesion with incomplete ring enhancement open toward the cortex, little mass effect, and few symptoms. Which feature best favors tumefactive demyelination over glioma?
options: A closed thick irregular ring with central necrosis
An open ring of enhancement with minimal mass effect
Marked surrounding mass effect with midline shift present
Rapid growth over several days on repeat MRI scans
items.explanation: An incomplete ring open toward the cortex or basal ganglia, with limited mass effect and edema relative to size, suggests tumefactive demyelination. A closed irregular necrotic ring, severe mass effect, and rapid growth raise concern for glioblastoma or lymphoma. Spectroscopy and, when unclear, biopsy settle uncertain cases. Advanced imaging, including spectroscopy and perfusion, and a careful trial of corticosteroids guide management, while biopsy is reserved for cases where the diagnosis remains uncertain.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis has had two severe optic neuritis attacks while taking natalizumab. Serum testing is positive for aquaporin-4 antibodies. What is the best action?
options: Stop natalizumab and start an NMOSD therapy such as rituximab
Increase the natalizumab dosing frequency to every two weeks
Add interferon beta to the current natalizumab regimen
Continue the current regimen unchanged and repeat the MRI in a year
items.explanation: Positive aquaporin-4 IgG establishes NMOSD, and several multiple sclerosis drugs, including natalizumab, interferon beta, and fingolimod, can worsen it. The drug should be replaced with an NMOSD-directed agent such as rituximab or an approved alternative. Intensifying or combining multiple sclerosis therapy risks further attacks and permanent disability. Seronegative patients still need careful evaluation, but with a positive antibody the diagnosis is established and relapse prevention should begin with an agent proven to help.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has weight loss, diarrhea, arthralgias, dementia, and slow rhythmic convergent eye oscillations with jaw movements. Which treatment is best?
options: Short course of oral amoxicillin
Intravenous acyclovir for 14 days
Corticosteroids as monotherapy
Ceftriaxone induction followed by prolonged trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
items.explanation: Oculomasticatory myorhythmia is nearly pathognomonic for CNS Whipple disease from Tropheryma whipplei, treated with a CNS-penetrating induction regimen such as ceftriaxone followed by about a year of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Brief amoxicillin relapses, acyclovir treats herpesviruses, and steroids worsen infection. Early recognition is crucial because untreated disease is fatal, and the combination of gastrointestinal and joint symptoms with these eye and jaw movements points to the correct diagnosis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has fever, neck stiffness, and confusion. CSF Gram stain is pending. What empiric regimen is best?
options: Ceftriaxone alone with no adjunct
Ampicillin and gentamicin without steroids
Vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and ampicillin, with dexamethasone given before or with the first antibiotic dose
Oral amoxicillin with fluid restriction
items.explanation: Adults over 50 need coverage for resistant pneumococcus with vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin, and ampicillin for Listeria. Dexamethasone given early improves outcomes, mainly in pneumococcal disease. Ceftriaxone alone misses Listeria and resistant strains, and oral therapy is inadequate for meningitis. Ampicillin is added because Listeria is more common at older ages, and steroids are stopped if cultures do not show pneumococcus, so the regimen is adjusted once organisms are identified.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has brief faciobrachial dystonic seizures, then memory loss and a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L. Which antibody is most likely?
options: Glycine receptor antibody with stiff-person features
Anti-Ma2 antibody with brainstem encephalitis
Amphiphysin antibody with paraneoplastic syndrome
Leucine-rich glioma inactivated 1 antibody
items.explanation: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures and hyponatremia with limbic encephalitis are classic for anti-LGI1 encephalitis, which often responds well to immunotherapy. Glycine receptor antibodies cause stiff-person spectrum disorders, anti-Ma2 causes brainstem and limbic encephalitis in testicular cancer, and amphiphysin antibodies cause stiff-person syndrome with cancer. These patients usually improve with immunotherapy, and recognizing the seizure type and low sodium early allows treatment before irreversible hippocampal damage occurs.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with multiple sclerosis wants to improve his walking speed. Which condition is a contraindication to dalfampridine?
options: Spasticity that is being treated with baclofen
History of seizures or moderate to severe renal impairment
Fatigue that is being treated with amantadine
Bladder urgency treated with an anticholinergic agent and fluids
items.explanation: Dalfampridine, a potassium channel blocker, lowers the seizure threshold and is renally cleared, so seizure history and creatinine clearance of 50 mL per minute or less are contraindications. Baclofen, amantadine, and anticholinergics are symptomatic agents that do not preclude its use. Walking speed gains occur in a subset of responders, and creatinine clearance is estimated first because accumulation raises the chance of seizures and other neurologic adverse effects.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man has double vision on looking to the left. The left eye fails to adduct, and the right eye shows abducting nystagmus, while convergence is preserved. Which structure is injured?
options: Left medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons
Left abducens nucleus in the caudal pontine tegmentum
Right oculomotor nerve fascicle in the midbrain
Left paramedian pontine reticular formation
items.explanation: Failure of adduction on the side of the lesion with contralateral abducting nystagmus is internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion, and preserved convergence places it in the pons. In a young adult it strongly suggests multiple sclerosis. An abducens nucleus lesion causes a gaze palsy, and the paramedian reticular formation causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man with multiple sclerosis has mild numbness of one hand for three days that does not affect his work or function. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Plasma exchange for any new symptom
Observation, since steroids speed recovery but do not change long-term outcome
Admission for high-dose methylprednisolone in every case
Immediate switch to a more potent disease therapy
items.explanation: Steroids shorten relapse duration but do not improve eventual disability, so mild nondisabling relapses may be managed expectantly after excluding infection. Plasma exchange is reserved for severe relapses unresponsive to steroids. Treating every symptom wastes resources and exposes patients to adverse effects, and a new relapse alone does not mandate escalation unless activity is repeated.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and ataxia over three months. MRI shows cortical ribboning on diffusion imaging. Which CSF test is the most specific?
options: Real-time quaking-induced conversion assay
Oligoclonal band analysis in the spinal fluid
Cell count and glucose measurement alone
VDRL testing with treponemal confirmation
items.explanation: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is supported by diffusion MRI cortical ribboning and by the RT-QuIC assay, which has high sensitivity and nearly perfect specificity. 14-3-3 protein is less specific. Oligoclonal bands, cell count, and VDRL address inflammatory or infectious disorders and do not confirm prion disease. Diffusion MRI, electroencephalography, and the 14-3-3 protein add supportive information, but the amyloid conversion assay has the best specificity, and the diagnosis is confirmed at autopsy.

items.stem: A 26-year-old man has bilateral optic neuritis with marked optic disc swelling and perineural enhancement, and aquaporin-4 antibodies are negative. Which result most likely explains this picture?
options: Positive anti-Hu antibody in serum, indicating paraneoplastic neuronopathy
Elevated CSF 14-3-3 protein with rapidly progressive dementia
Positive myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein IgG on a cell-based assay
Positive serum treponemal antibody with a reactive CSF VDRL test
items.explanation: Bilateral, anterior, long segment optic neuritis with disc edema and perineural enhancement, and often better visual recovery, is typical of MOG antibody disease. Cell-based assays are the preferred test. Anti-Hu indicates paraneoplastic neuronopathy, 14-3-3 supports prion disease, and a positive treponemal test would only suggest syphilis with a different presentation. Antibody testing with a live cell-based assay avoids false positives, and relapses may occur, so follow-up decisions about long-term therapy depend on relapse behavior.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man has depression, painful sensory symptoms, and then ataxia. MRI shows bilateral pulvinar hyperintensity. Which disease is likely?
options: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
Wernicke encephalopathy
Herpes simplex encephalitis
Variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease linked to bovine spongiform encephalopathy
items.explanation: Variant disease affects younger patients with early psychiatric symptoms and the pulvinar sign, and it is associated with consumption of contaminated beef. Sporadic disease occurs in older adults with rapid dementia and myoclonus, Wernicke has a nutritional cause, and herpes encephalitis involves the temporal lobes. Because transmission occurred through dietary exposure in the past, a history of residence in affected countries and the characteristic MRI help distinguish this entity from sporadic disease.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman on interferon beta has flu-like symptoms for hours after each injection. What is the best advice?
options: Stop all disease therapy permanently
Take an antipyretic analgesic before injecting and consider gradual dose titration
Add daily high-dose prednisone
Convert to monthly plasma exchange
items.explanation: Flu-like symptoms are the commonest interferon adverse effect and usually fade over months, and acetaminophen or ibuprofen taken beforehand, evening injection, and dose titration reduce them. Permanent withdrawal is premature. Daily steroids and plasma exchange are inappropriate, since this is a tolerability problem rather than disease activity. Neutralizing antibodies and liver enzyme elevations are also followed, but the flu-like reaction is the main reason patients abandon therapy early in treatment.

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy develops fever, drowsiness, and ataxia two weeks after a viral illness. MRI shows large bilateral poorly marginated T2 lesions in the white matter and thalami. What is the initial treatment?
options: Long-term interferon beta injections
Intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses monthly
Oral antiviral therapy alone for ten days
High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone
items.explanation: This is acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a usually monophasic post-infectious demyelinating illness with encephalopathy and multifocal deficits. First-line therapy is high-dose corticosteroids, with immunoglobulin or plasma exchange for failure. Interferon beta is a chronic multiple sclerosis therapy, cyclophosphamide is not first-line, and antivirals do not treat the immune mechanism. Most children recover well, and a second event after steroids should prompt testing for MOG antibody disease or evolving multiple sclerosis rather than assuming a repeat of the first illness.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man starts dimethyl fumarate. Which laboratory measurement is most important for ongoing safety monitoring?
options: Absolute lymphocyte count
Serum creatinine kinase
Thyroid stimulating hormone
Platelet antibody titer
items.explanation: Dimethyl fumarate can cause lymphopenia, and prolonged severe lymphopenia is linked to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, so complete blood counts are checked regularly. Flushing and abdominal symptoms are the common tolerability issues. Thyroid disease is a concern with alemtuzumab, and creatine kinase and platelet antibodies are not routine monitoring for this agent. Flushing and gastrointestinal upset usually improve over weeks, and taking the capsule with food or aspirin beforehand reduces flushing in many patients.

items.stem: After natalizumab was stopped and plasma exchange used to remove it during PML, a patient worsens with new enhancing lesions and edema around the old ones. What is the most likely cause and treatment?
options: Natalizumab rebound neuromyelitis optica treated with interferon
Cryptococcal meningitis treated with fluconazole
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome treated with corticosteroids
Stroke treated with thrombolysis
items.explanation: Rapid restoration of immune function after drug removal can provoke an inflammatory response against JC virus antigen, producing new enhancement and edema. Corticosteroids are used for significant cases. Interferon would not help, cryptococcosis and stroke are not suggested by the course, and thrombolysis would be hazardous. Management is supportive and anti-inflammatory, and worsening after removal of the drug should not be mistaken for natalizumab failure or a new relapse of multiple sclerosis.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has severe ear pain, a facial palsy, and vesicles in the external ear canal. What is the best treatment?
options: Oral amoxicillin alone
Oral valacyclovir plus prednisone
Intravenous ceftriaxone
Surgical decompression of the facial nerve
items.explanation: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is facial palsy from varicella zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion, treated with an antiviral and corticosteroids to improve recovery. Antibiotics do not act on the virus, and surgical decompression is not first-line. Early treatment improves the chance of facial recovery, and delayed therapy beyond three days lowers the likelihood of complete return of function and increases the risk of synkinesis.

items.stem: A 38-year-old Black woman has intractable hiccups and vomiting, followed by a myelitis spanning six vertebral segments. Which structure explains the first symptoms?
options: Area postrema in the dorsal medulla
Nucleus ambiguus in the ventrolateral medulla
Pontine tegmentum near the locus coeruleus
Red nucleus in the midbrain
items.explanation: Area postrema syndrome, with hiccups, nausea, and vomiting, is a core clinical feature of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder because this region lacks a tight blood-brain barrier and is rich in aquaporin-4. The nucleus ambiguus governs swallowing and phonation, and the pons and red nucleus do not produce this presentation. Recognizing area postrema syndrome matters because it can be the first manifestation, and antibody testing should follow even when the spinal cord is initially spared.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with highly active multiple sclerosis is offered cladribine. Which description of its use is correct?
options: Daily oral dosing with monthly liver tests and contraception
A weekly subcutaneous injection given by the patient at home
A single intravenous infusion repeated every six months in clinic
Two short oral courses a year apart that deplete lymphocytes
items.explanation: Cladribine tablets are given as two yearly treatment courses, each lasting a few days over two consecutive months, producing selective lymphocyte reduction. Lymphocyte counts are monitored and malignancy screening is advised. Daily dosing describes teriflunomide, weekly injection is not a regimen for this drug, and six-monthly infusion is the ocrelizumab schedule. Its immune effect persists beyond the dosing period, so lymphocyte counts, infection screening, and age-appropriate cancer screening are part of long-term follow-up.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman will begin ocrelizumab. Which test is most important before the first infusion?
options: Serum anti-JC virus index
Electrocardiogram
Hepatitis B serology
Varicella antibody titer only
items.explanation: Anti-CD20 therapies can reactivate hepatitis B, so surface antigen and core antibody are checked before treatment. The JC virus index informs natalizumab risk. An electrocardiogram is used for sphingosine receptor modulators. Varicella immunity matters for fingolimod and alemtuzumab, but does not address the reactivation hazard of B cell depletion. Infusion reactions and low immunoglobulin levels over time are additional monitored risks, so infection history and immunoglobulin measurement guide long-term safety decisions.

items.stem: A pathologist reviews tissue from a patient with Balo concentric sclerosis. Which finding is characteristic?
options: Alternating concentric bands of demyelination and preserved myelin
Cytoplasmic neuronal inclusions with spongiform change
Perivascular granulomas with giant cells
Diffuse amyloid deposition in leptomeningeal vessels
items.explanation: Balo concentric sclerosis shows rings of demyelinated tissue alternating with relatively preserved myelin, giving an onion bulb pattern on MRI. Spongiform change belongs to prion disease, granulomas with giant cells suggest sarcoidosis or tuberculosis, and amyloid in vessels suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Marburg disease is the acute fulminant form, treated with high-dose steroids and plasma exchange, and Balo sclerosis may respond similarly while later therapy follows multiple sclerosis principles.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 40 has headache and hemiparesis, and MRI shows several ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesions. What is the best empiric therapy?
options: Whole brain radiation therapy for presumed lymphoma
Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin
Amphotericin B for fungal disease
Intravenous cidofovir for viral disease
items.explanation: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in a patient with advanced HIV suggest toxoplasmosis, and empiric therapy with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine plus leucovorin is given with reassessment at about two weeks. Radiation treats lymphoma and amphotericin B treats fungi, while cidofovir has no role. Clinical and radiographic response within about two weeks confirms the diagnosis, and a biopsy is considered only if the lesions fail to improve on the empiric regimen.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has a spinal cord MRI showing a longitudinal central T2 lesion spanning only two vertebral segments with peripheral dorsal location. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Lesions under three segments exclude demyelination
Central lesions are typical of multiple sclerosis
Short peripheral lesions are typical of multiple sclerosis, whereas long central lesions suggest NMOSD
Cord lesions are rare in multiple sclerosis
items.explanation: Multiple sclerosis lesions are usually short, under two vertebral segments, and located in the peripheral dorsal or lateral cord. Longitudinally extensive central lesions spanning three or more segments suggest NMOSD. Short lesions do not exclude demyelination, and cord involvement is common in multiple sclerosis. Recognizing this pattern keeps the diagnosis correct, because an extensive central lesion would instead point toward aquaporin-4 antibody disease, where treatment and prognosis differ substantially.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a first episode of painful monocular vision loss. Brain MRI shows several T2 lesions. Which finding best satisfies dissemination in space under the current McDonald criteria?
options: Two or more enhancing lesions confined to the periventricular white matter
One large lesion in the optic nerve that enhances with gadolinium
Three or more T2 lesions anywhere in the supratentorial white matter
One or more T2 lesions in at least two of four typical regions: periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord
items.explanation: The 2017 McDonald criteria require lesions in at least two of four characteristic locations to show dissemination in space. Optic nerve lesions count as a symptomatic site but the criterion is regional spread. Multiple lesions confined to one region, even if enhancing or numerous, do not satisfy it, because the rule counts distinct anatomic territories rather than lesion number.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with aggressive multiple sclerosis received mitoxantrone for two years. What must be monitored and limited?
options: Cumulative lifetime dose with left ventricular ejection fraction
Cumulative pulmonary dose with serial pulmonary function tests only
Serum sodium with serum osmolality checks
Hearing thresholds with serial audiometry testing
items.explanation: Mitoxantrone is cardiotoxic, so ejection fraction is checked before each dose and the cumulative lifetime dose is capped at about 140 mg per square meter. It also carries a risk of therapy-related acute leukemia. Pulmonary toxicity, hyponatremia, and ototoxicity are not its limiting concerns. Heart failure and secondary leukemia can appear years later, so treatment is reserved for patients with highly active disease who have exhausted safer options.

items.stem: A hiker wakes to find a bat on his arm, and no bite is visible. What is the correct management?
options: Observation only because there is no visible bite wound
Oral antibiotics for five days to prevent bacterial wound infection
A single tetanus booster injection and no other treatment
Wound washing, rabies immune globulin, and the vaccine series
items.explanation: Bat exposure without a visible bite, such as a sleeping person, warrants post-exposure prophylaxis because small bat bites go unnoticed, and rabies is nearly always fatal once symptoms start. Prophylaxis includes wound care, immune globulin, and the vaccine series. Observation, antibiotics, and tetanus alone do not prevent rabies. Prophylaxis must start as soon as possible, because once symptoms begin the disease is almost uniformly fatal, and testing the animal is not possible when it escapes.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman stops natalizumab after a positive JC antibody result and receives no other therapy. Which outcome is the main concern in the following months?
options: Immediate permanent remission
Sudden onset of neuromyelitis optica
Rebound disease activity, so a replacement high-efficacy therapy should be planned
Reversible hepatotoxicity requiring transplantation
items.explanation: Stopping natalizumab can unmask severe rebound activity within months, sometimes exceeding pretreatment levels, so a transition therapy is planned in advance. Remission does not follow withdrawal. NMOSD is not a result of stopping the drug, and hepatotoxicity, although reported, is not the principal concern. Switching to ocrelizumab, a sphingosine receptor modulator, or another agent soon after withdrawal reduces rebound, and MRI and clinical follow-up should be scheduled closely.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has typical features of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, but serum antibodies are negative. What best explains this?
options: The diagnosis is excluded by negative serum testing
Cerebrospinal fluid is more sensitive than serum, so spinal fluid testing is required
Antibodies are present only after tumor removal
Serum testing is the most sensitive method
items.explanation: In NMDA receptor encephalitis, antibody testing in CSF is more sensitive and specific than in serum, and serum can be falsely negative, so CSF should always be sent. Negative serum does not exclude the disease, and antibodies do not appear only after tumor removal. Negative serum with positive spinal fluid is not rare, so a high clinical suspicion should drive lumbar puncture, even when the first antibody result is reassuring.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has a progressive pancerebellar syndrome with negative onconeural antibodies, and chest and abdominal CT show no mass. Which test should be done next if cancer is suspected?
options: Whole-body FDG-PET
Repeat the CT after a decade
Bone scan only
Brain biopsy
items.explanation: Paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes often precede the tumor, which may be too small for CT, and FDG-PET is more sensitive at finding occult cancer. Waiting a decade is unsafe, a bone scan targets only skeletal disease, and brain biopsy is not indicated. Mammography or pelvic imaging are added when appropriate for the antibody and demographics, and repeat screening continues at intervals when the first studies are negative.

items.stem: A neurologist selects maintenance therapy for aquaporin-4 positive NMOSD with a monoclonal antibody that depletes B cells by targeting CD19. Which agent is this?
options: Natalizumab
Interferon beta-1a
Inebilizumab
Fingolimod
items.explanation: Inebilizumab binds CD19 and is approved to prevent relapses in aquaporin-4 positive NMOSD, alongside eculizumab and satralizumab, with rituximab used off label. Natalizumab, interferon beta, and fingolimod are multiple sclerosis agents that may worsen NMOSD and should be avoided. Eculizumab targets complement component C5 and satralizumab blocks the interleukin 6 receptor, so several mechanisms are available for aquaporin-4 positive disease.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man returns from Nigeria with fever, then becomes comatose with seizures. Smear shows Plasmodium falciparum with high parasitemia. What is the best treatment?
options: Oral chloroquine alone
Intravenous artesunate
Intravenous ceftriaxone
Dexamethasone
items.explanation: Cerebral malaria is a medical emergency, and intravenous artesunate is first-line for severe falciparum malaria. Chloroquine is inadequate because of widespread resistance and the severity of illness, ceftriaxone does not treat parasites, and dexamethasone worsens outcomes in cerebral malaria. Supportive care for seizures, glucose, and intracranial pressure continues, and follow-on oral therapy completes the course after the patient is able to take medication.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has lightning pains, ataxia, and small pupils that constrict to accommodation but not to light. Serum testing is positive and CSF VDRL is reactive. What is the best treatment?
options: Single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin
Oral doxycycline for 14 days
Oral azithromycin for 5 days
Intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days
items.explanation: Neurosyphilis with tabes dorsalis and Argyll Robertson pupils is treated with intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days to reach treponemicidal CNS levels. A single benzathine dose does not achieve adequate CSF concentration, and oral alternatives lack proven efficacy for neurosyphilis. Benzathine penicillin does not reach adequate concentrations in spinal fluid, so intravenous therapy is required, and follow-up CSF testing documents response after treatment is complete.

items.stem: A 60-year-old heavy smoker has months of asymmetric painful sensory loss, sensory ataxia, and areflexia. What is the most likely antibody and tumor?
options: Anti-Yo (PCA-1) with breast or ovarian cancer
Anti-Ri (ANNA-2) with thymoma in older men
Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) with small cell lung cancer
Anti-CV2 (CRMP5) with Hodgkin lymphoma
items.explanation: Subacute painful sensory neuronopathy from dorsal root ganglion injury is the classic anti-Hu syndrome, associated with small cell lung cancer, and it often accompanies encephalomyelitis. Anti-Yo is linked to cerebellar degeneration in gynecologic tumors, and anti-Ri to opsoclonus and brainstem syndromes. Prognosis is poor because neurons are destroyed by cytotoxic T cells, so detecting and treating the tumor early is the main therapeutic opportunity available.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has encephalopathy, high-frequency hearing loss, and headaches. MRI shows small central lesions of the corpus callosum, and fundoscopy shows a branch retinal artery occlusion. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Susac syndrome
Relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
items.explanation: The triad of encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss with central callosal lesions defines Susac syndrome, a microangiopathy of brain, retina, and cochlea. Multiple sclerosis does not cause retinal arterial occlusion. ADEM is monophasic and follows infection, and NMOSD causes optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis rather than hearing loss and retinal infarcts.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man has memory loss, seizures, and brainstem signs, with MRI showing bilateral medial temporal T2 hyperintensity. Anti-Ma2 antibodies are positive. Which cancer should be sought?
options: Ovarian teratoma of the pelvis
Testicular germ cell tumor
Thymoma of the anterior mediastinum
Hodgkin lymphoma of nodes
items.explanation: Anti-Ma2 encephalitis affects young men with testicular germ cell tumors, causing limbic, diencephalic, and brainstem dysfunction, and testicular ultrasound is recommended. Ovarian teratoma pairs with NMDA receptor antibodies, thymoma with several syndromes, and Hodgkin lymphoma with anti-Tr cerebellar degeneration. Early recognition matters because treating the testicular tumor and giving immunotherapy can stabilize neurologic function, although outcomes remain worse than with cell-surface antibody syndromes.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has subacute encephalopathy, tremor, and myoclonus. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are elevated, other causes are excluded, and she improves with corticosteroids. What is the diagnosis?
options: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease with prion protein accumulation in cortex
Hepatic encephalopathy from advanced cirrhosis
Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency state
Steroid-responsive encephalopathy with autoimmune thyroiditis
items.explanation: Hashimoto encephalopathy, now called SREAT, is a diagnosis of exclusion with raised thyroid antibodies and a dramatic steroid response, though the antibodies are common in healthy people. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease fails to respond to steroids, and hepatic and Wernicke encephalopathy have metabolic and nutritional causes. Because antithyroid antibodies are found in many healthy adults, the label should be applied cautiously after excluding infection, other autoimmune encephalitis, and metabolic causes.

items.stem: A 27-year-old immigrant from rural Central America has a first seizure, and CT shows a cystic lesion with an eccentric dot. Which treatment is best?
options: Surgical removal of every cyst through repeated open craniotomies
Antibiotics for presumed brain abscess caused by bacteria
Albendazole with corticosteroids and an antiseizure medication
Observation without any drug therapy until seizures recur
items.explanation: A cyst with a scolex indicates viable neurocysticercosis, and treatment combines albendazole, steroids to blunt inflammation as the parasite dies, and seizure control. Routine surgery is not needed, abscess therapy is wrong, and observation leaves viable cysts to cause recurrent seizures. Steroids prevent inflammatory worsening as cysts die, and antiseizure medication controls the epileptic activity, while treatment of subarachnoid or ventricular disease may need extra measures.

items.stem: A 2-year-old girl has irritability, truncal ataxia, myoclonus, and chaotic multidirectional eye movements. Which evaluation is most important?
options: Lumbar puncture for 14-3-3 protein and real-time quaking-induced conversion testing
Chest and abdominal imaging with urine catecholamine metabolites
Genetic testing for ataxia telangiectasia mutations
Sweat chloride testing for cystic fibrosis
items.explanation: Opsoclonus myoclonus ataxia syndrome in a toddler is paraneoplastic or post-infectious, and neuroblastoma must be sought with imaging and urine catecholamines. 14-3-3 protein suggests prion disease, ataxia telangiectasia presents differently, and sweat chloride testing evaluates cystic fibrosis. Treatment combines tumor management with immunotherapy, and early therapy improves long-term cognitive outcomes in children, who often have lasting behavioral and sleep problems.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man is evaluated for suspected multiple sclerosis. Which spinal fluid result should most prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis?
options: Neutrophilic pleocytosis of 150 cells per microliter
Four CSF specific oligoclonal bands with elevated IgG index
A raised IgG index in a CSF sample with normal protein level
A lymphocytic pleocytosis of 8 cells per microliter in fluid
items.explanation: Multiple sclerosis typically shows a normal or mildly raised lymphocyte count, usually under 50 cells per microliter, with intrathecal IgG synthesis. A high count with neutrophil predominance should raise concern for infection, NMOSD, or another inflammatory process. Oligoclonal bands, a raised IgG index, and mild lymphocytic pleocytosis are all compatible with the diagnosis. A very high count, neutrophils, or markedly raised protein should prompt testing for infection, sarcoidosis, lymphoma, NMOSD, and other mimics before accepting the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman taking teriflunomide for multiple sclerosis learns that she is pregnant. Which immediate step is most appropriate?
options: Continue the drug until the second trimester
Switch to oral dalfampridine
Observe for a month because it clears quickly
Accelerated elimination with cholestyramine
items.explanation: Teriflunomide is teratogenic and has a very long half-life, so when pregnancy occurs or is planned, accelerated elimination with cholestyramine or activated charcoal is recommended. Continuing it exposes the fetus. Dalfampridine only improves walking and is not a disease therapy, and waiting is unsafe because the drug persists in plasma for months without washout. Hepatotoxicity and hair thinning are additional adverse effects, and men planning conception should also consider the drug and its washout before attempting paternity.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has muscle twitching, severe insomnia, profuse sweating, and confusion. Examination shows neuromyotonia, and chest CT shows an anterior mediastinal mass. Which antibody is most likely?
options: GABA-B receptor antibody, with lung cancer
Anti-Yo antibody, with ovarian cancer
CASPR2 antibody, with a thymoma
Anti-Hu antibody, with small cell cancer
items.explanation: Morvan syndrome combines peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, dysautonomia, insomnia, and encephalopathy, and is linked to CASPR2 antibodies and thymoma. GABA-B encephalitis presents with early seizures, anti-Yo with cerebellar degeneration, and anti-Hu with sensory neuronopathy and encephalomyelitis, so none matches this picture. Because thymoma can be missed on plain radiographs, cross-sectional imaging of the chest is needed, and removal of the tumor combined with immunotherapy improves outcomes.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman starts fingolimod. Which adverse effect is most likely during the first hours after the initial dose and requires monitoring?
options: Macular edema appearing within a few weeks of treatment
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy from viral reactivation
Hepatic necrosis requiring urgent liver transplant
Bradycardia and atrioventricular conduction delay
items.explanation: Sphingosine 1 phosphate receptor modulators transiently slow heart rate and conduction after the first dose, so patients are monitored for about six hours with electrocardiography. Macular edema and infections such as PML or cryptococcal disease appear later, and hepatic injury is a monitored risk of other agents, not the first-dose concern. Contraindications include recent myocardial infarction, certain heart block, and some antiarrhythmic drugs, so an electrocardiogram and ophthalmologic baseline are obtained before starting.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has weeks of pancerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, and downbeat nystagmus. MRI is initially normal, and she has anti-Yo antibodies. Which cancer should be sought first?
options: Breast or ovarian cancer
Prostate adenocarcinoma
Colorectal adenocarcinoma
Renal cell carcinoma tumor
items.explanation: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with anti-Yo (PCA-1) antibodies occurs mainly in women with breast or gynecologic cancer, and the neurologic syndrome often precedes the tumor. The other cancers listed are not typical associations, and Purkinje cell loss leaves little recovery even with tumor treatment. The antibody often appears before the tumor is found, so surveillance imaging is repeated, and Purkinje cell loss means recovery is limited even if the cancer is removed.

items.stem: A 12-year-old with cyanotic congenital heart disease has fever, headache, and a single ring-enhancing frontal lesion. What is the best next step?
options: High-dose corticosteroids alone
Neurosurgical aspiration for culture with empiric intravenous antibiotics
Lumbar puncture before any imaging review
Antiepileptic therapy only
items.explanation: A right-to-left shunt bypasses pulmonary filtration and predisposes to brain abscess, which is managed with drainage or aspiration for culture and prolonged intravenous antibiotics. Steroids alone risk worsening infection, lumbar puncture risks herniation, and antiseizure therapy is supportive only. Cultures guide narrowing of antibiotics, and drainage reduces mass effect and permits an organism to be identified, while steroids are limited to patients with significant edema.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman in the northeastern United States has meningitis with painful radiculitis and CSF lymphocytosis, and Lyme serology is positive. What is the recommended treatment?
options: Oral amoxicillin for three days
Topical permethrin
No treatment, because it resolves spontaneously
Intravenous ceftriaxone
items.explanation: Lyme neuroborreliosis with meningitis and radiculitis is treated with parenteral ceftriaxone for about two to four weeks, and oral doxycycline is an alternative in some forms. A very short oral course is inadequate, permethrin is a scabicide, and untreated disease may progress to chronic neurologic deficits. Early disease responds well to antibiotics, and facial palsy without meningitis can often be treated with an oral agent, but CNS involvement with meningitis calls for parenteral treatment.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a two-year history of slowly worsening spastic paraparesis without any discrete relapse. MRI shows spinal cord atrophy and a few brain lesions, and CSF has oligoclonal bands. What is the best classification?
options: Secondary progressive multiple sclerosis
Clinically isolated syndrome
Primary progressive multiple sclerosis
Relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis with active disease
items.explanation: Progressive worsening from onset, without a preceding relapsing course, defines primary progressive multiple sclerosis, and spinal cord involvement with intrathecal oligoclonal bands supports it. Secondary progression requires an earlier relapsing phase. A clinically isolated syndrome is a single acute episode, and relapsing remitting disease requires discrete attacks with recovery. Recognizing the progressive phenotype early matters because relapse-targeted drugs offer less benefit and ocrelizumab is the approved option.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with migraine has an MRI that shows several ovoid periventricular and juxtacortical T2 lesions meeting dissemination criteria. She has never had neurologic symptoms. What is the correct term?
options: Radiologically isolated syndrome
Clinically isolated syndrome
Relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis
Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease
items.explanation: Incidental MRI findings typical of demyelination in a person without symptoms or signs define radiologically isolated syndrome. A clinically isolated syndrome needs a first symptomatic episode, and relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis requires clinical relapses or the McDonald definition in a symptomatic patient. MOG antibody disease is defined by antibody status plus a compatible clinical event.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man in August has fever, then acute asymmetric flaccid weakness of one arm with preserved sensation. MRI shows anterior horn changes and CSF is lymphocytic. Which test is most useful?
options: Serum anti-ganglioside antibodies
CSF West Nile virus IgM
CSF 14-3-3 protein
Nerve conduction without CSF testing
items.explanation: Asymmetric flaccid paralysis with fever in summer indicates poliomyelitis-like anterior horn cell damage from West Nile virus, confirmed by CSF IgM. Anti-ganglioside antibodies relate to Guillain-Barre syndrome, 14-3-3 to prion disease, and conduction studies alone would not give the cause. Supportive care is the mainstay since no antiviral has proven benefit, and prognosis for recovery of the paralyzed limb is often limited, so early recognition guides counseling.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has days of anxiety and psychosis, then seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, and autonomic instability. Which investigation is most important after confirming the diagnosis?
options: Testicular ultrasound for germ cell tumor
Colonoscopy for colorectal carcinoma
Thyroid biopsy for papillary carcinoma
Pelvic imaging for ovarian teratoma
items.explanation: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in young women is often associated with ovarian teratoma, and tumor removal speeds recovery. Testicular ultrasound would apply to anti-Ma2 syndrome in men, colonoscopy and thyroid biopsy are not the usual cancer searches. Early identification and tumor resection combined with immunotherapy leads to better recovery, so the search for a teratoma continues even if the first scan is unrevealing.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with active secondary progressive multiple sclerosis is to start siponimod. Which test must be performed first?
options: CYP2C9 genotype
HLA B27 typing
Serum aquaporin-4 antibody level
Thiopurine methyltransferase activity
items.explanation: Siponimod is metabolized mainly by CYP2C9, and patients with the 3/3 genotype cannot receive it, with dose adjustment for the 1/3 and 2/3 genotypes. Ophthalmic and cardiac assessments are also done. HLA typing, aquaporin antibodies, and thiopurine methyltransferase activity have no role in its prescribing. Dose and eligibility depend on genotype because reduced clearance raises drug exposure, and cardiac conduction and macular assessment are also part of the baseline evaluation.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis had no relapses during her pregnancy. She asks when her risk of relapse is highest. What is the best answer?
options: During the first trimester of the pregnancy itself
During the third trimester just before delivery
In the first three months after delivery
Evenly across the entire pregnancy period
items.explanation: Relapse rates fall in the third trimester, likely through pregnancy-related immune tolerance, then rebound in the first months postpartum. Pregnancy overall is not a time of increased risk, and the first trimester resembles baseline. Counseling about restarting disease therapy and breastfeeding plans before delivery is the practical response to the postpartum rise. Counseling before delivery should cover restarting disease therapy and whether breastfeeding fits the chosen agent, since postpartum protection depends on planning.

items.stem: A 64-year-old smoker has rapid onset of limbic encephalitis with refractory seizures early in the course. Which antibody and tumor association is most likely?
options: AMPA receptor antibody and renal cell carcinoma of kidney
GABA-B receptor antibody and small cell lung carcinoma
Anti-Tr antibody and colon adenocarcinoma
Anti-Yo antibody and bladder carcinoma
items.explanation: GABA-B receptor encephalitis causes prominent early seizures with limbic features and is associated with small cell lung cancer in about half of cases. AMPA receptor encephalitis links to thymoma, breast, and lung tumors, anti-Tr to Hodgkin lymphoma, and anti-Yo to gynecologic and breast tumors. Chest imaging and PET are used to find the lung tumor, and treating the cancer along with immunotherapy offers the best chance of recovery.
